chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: His current band: saxophonist-flutist Sports Lewis
summary: Horace plays Hammond organ in a four-piece group with a vocalist; Sports Lewis from Philadelphia plays tenor and flute and screams at the end of his Swinging Shepherd Blues.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: How many do you have in your group?

I have four members, including myself; but I have three musicians and a vocalist. I'm playing the Hammond organ and two (unintelligible) speakers. Of course, that is a B-2 would be two, and I have an excellent saxophonist that doubles on the flute named Sports Lewis, and he's actually an easterner. He's from around Philadelphia (unintelligible), Pennsylvania, and he's been playing for quite a few years. Plays an excellent flute, plays a very good swing tenor tune, and he's a good reader, and he's learned my style with this particular group that I wanted. And he fits in very nicely.
Uh-huh. How old a man is he?
Oh, I would say Sports is towards in his late '30's, middle '30's, I would say.
Has he played with any name bands that you know of?
Back east he said he has played with some groups around Philadelphia. In fact, he's a very good friend of -- you remember the guy that wrote // 720 // -- not // 720, -- "720 in the Books,"
728, in the books?
Bon Bon, Loren-Barn, with that great band, Jan Savitt --
Right.
-- years ago in Philadelphia? Well, he knows Loren-Barn, you know, and of course, Bon Bon (unintelligible).

I think in recent later years has only been active as a deejay around Philadelphia, but he knew him in his early years, and was a little when he was stinker, man -- a little kid going to school. (unintelligible) stricken with a stroke. And we talk about it sometimes, and I think they must have gone to the same school, you know. And he often frequented a lot of places where jazz was at its best.
There's a club that he talked about in Philadelphia -- is it Pepsi's of Pep's?
I don't --
It's one of the two, but nevertheless, jazz was quite fluent there, and he said that the great musicians out of New York come down and play there.
Is it Peppy's?

Peppy's -- it could have been, yes, (unintelligible). I don't know where it's located, but it's in the heart of town in Philadelphia, and Sports always talked about that, and it was his home town, you know. But he's real hip (unintelligible). He plays modern -- he's got a good, big tone, and he plays good ballads, and, of course, he plays good swing. And he plays He's on the beat. I like that.
Yeah, right on top.

And we've got two or three things we made up (unintelligible) quite a bit, and he really shows himself off fairly good. And he's got a thing that sometimes if you ever get have a chance to come up to Fort Collins, I want you to hear him play his version of
"The Swinging Shepherd Blues" on the flute.
(Singing)
And (unintelligible). He plays it like -- about 20 choruses and he plays them all different.
(Laughter)
And it's got a good beat on it, and about the last two choruses he lets out a big scream right on the end and frightens everybody in the house, just haa-aa-ah, right out loud, you know.
(Laughter)
He does that with his voice?

He does that with his voice, while holding his flute, all the same time. And then he'll play a little riff, and he'll get to moving, you know, and get the people swinging, you know, and he says, "Now I don't want you girls to get excited behind this," he says. "I see it's getting to you." So he talks -- he's funny, you know, and it -- you know, he sells it.
